T7A01: Sensitivity = the ability to detect weak signals. Selectivity = the ability to separate them.
T7A02: A transceiver is a transmitter and receiver in one box.
T7A03: A mixer converts a signal from one frequency to another.
T7A04: Selectivity = picking out one signal among many.
T7A05: An oscillator generates a signal at a set frequency.
T7A06: A transverter converts a rig's RF input and output to another band.
T7A07: PTT (push to talk): grounding it switches the rig to transmit.
T7A08: Putting speech onto a carrier = modulation.
T7A09: The SSB / CW-FM switch sets the amplifier to operate properly for that mode (linear for SSB).
T7A10: An RF power amplifier boosts the output power.
T7A11: The VFO sets the receive and transmit frequency.
T7B01: Over-deviating means too loud: back off from the mic.
T7B02: The broadcast receiver can't reject your strong signal outside its band. That's the receiver's weakness (overload).
T7B03: All of these cause RFI: fundamental overload, harmonics, spurious emissions.
T7B04: Solid-state rigs cut power when SWR is high, to protect themselves.
T7B05: Put a filter at the affected receiver's antenna input to block your signal.
T7B06: First, check your own station: does it interfere with your own TV or radio?
T7B07: A band-reject filter blocks the FM broadcast signal from your 2 m rig.
T7B08: All of these: work with the neighbor, politely mention the FCC rules, and see whether the device can be fixed.
T7B09: Cable TV interference: start by checking that every coax connector is installed properly.
T7B10: All of these can distort your audio through a repeater: off frequency, too loud or too close to the mic, or a bad location.
T7B11: RF feeding back into the rig distorts audio. A clip-on ferrite choke on the mic cable stops it.
T7C01: A dummy load lets you test without radiating a signal.
T7C02: An antenna analyzer shows whether an antenna is resonant where you want it.
T7C03: A dummy load = a 50-ohm non-inductive resistor on a heat sink.
T7C05: Rigs cut power at high SWR to protect the output transistors.
T7C07: Power lost in feed line turns into heat.
T7C08: A directional wattmeter (forward and reflected power) shows SWR. Iambic pentameter is poetry.
T7C09: Coax fails mostly from moisture getting in.
T7C10: UV light breaks down the jacket, which lets water in.
T7C11: Foam-dielectric coax has less loss per foot.
T7D01: Electric potential (voltage) is measured with a voltmeter.
T7D02: A voltmeter connects in parallel, across the component.
T7D03: To measure current, connect in series, so the current flows through the meter.
T7D04: Current is measured with an ammeter.
T7D05: An ohmmeter sends a small current through and measures the voltage that results.
T7D06: Measuring voltage on the resistance setting can damage the meter.
T7D07: A multimeter measures voltage and resistance (and current).
T7D08: Never use acid-core solder on electronics: it corrodes. Use rosin-core.
T7D09: A cold solder joint looks rough or lumpy. A good one is smooth and shiny.
T7D10: A discharged capacitor charges from the ohmmeter, so the resistance reading climbs over time.
T7D11: Measure resistance only with the circuit powered off.
T8A01: SSB is a form of AM.
T8A02: VHF packet radio uses FM or PM.
T8A03: SSB is the weak-signal, long-distance voice mode on VHF and UHF.
T8A06: 10 m and above use upper sideband (USB).
T8A08: SSB voice is about 3 kHz wide.
T8A09: FM voice on repeaters is 10-15 kHz wide.
T8A10: AM fast-scan TV is about 6 MHz wide, like an analog TV channel.
T8A12: FM's disadvantage: you only receive the strongest signal, one at a time (capture effect).
T8B01: Satellite beacons send telemetry on the satellite's health and status.
T8B02: Too much uplink power hogs the satellite and blocks other users.
T8B03: Tracking programs give all of these: maps, pass times with azimuth and elevation, and Doppler-shifted frequencies.
T8B04: Satellites use all of these modes: SSB, FM, CW, and data.
T8B05: A satellite beacon transmits status information.
T8B06: Tracking programs need the Keplerian elements (the numbers that define the orbit).
T8B07: Doppler shift: the frequency changes because the satellite is moving relative to you.
T8B08: U/V mode: UHF uplink (70 cm), VHF downlink (2 m).
T8B09: Spin fading comes from the satellite and its antennas rotating.
T8B10: LEO = low Earth orbit, about 100 minutes per orbit.
T8B12: Set your uplink power so your downlink signal is about as strong as the beacon.
T8C01: Find noise or jamming sources with radio direction finding.
T8C02: For a hidden transmitter hunt (fox hunt), you need a directional antenna.
T8C03: Contesting = contacting as many stations as possible in a set time.
T8C04: In contests, send only the minimum needed: your call and the exchange.
T8C05: A grid locator is a letter-number code for a geographic location (like FM17).
T8C06: Access IRLP nodes over the air using DTMF tones.
T8C07: VoIP = voice delivered over the internet digitally.
T8C08: IRLP links repeaters and other amateur systems over the internet.
T8C09: EchoLink lets you get into a repeater from a computer or phone, with no radio.
T8C10: EchoLink requires registering your call sign and proving you're licensed.
T8C11: A gateway connects amateur stations to the internet.
T8D01: All of these are digital modes: packet, IEEE 802.11 (Wi-Fi), and FT8.
T8D02: FT8 is a digital mode that works at very low signal-to-noise ratios.
T8D03: APRS can carry all of these: GPS position, text messages, and weather data.
T8D04: NTSC = analog fast-scan color TV (the old US TV standard).
T8D05: APRS: real-time tactical communications plus a map of station locations.
T8D07: DMR fits two voice signals on one 12.5 kHz channel using time slots.
T8D08: Packet radio includes all of these: a checksum, a header with the destination call sign, and automatic repeat requests (ARQ).
T8D10: WSJT-X supports all of these: EME, weak-signal beacons, and meteor scatter.
T8D11: ARQ: the receiver detects errors and asks for a retransmission.
T8D12: An amateur mesh network uses commercial Wi-Fi gear running modified firmware.
T9A01: A beam antenna concentrates the signal in one direction.
T9A02: Loading = adding inductors to make an antenna electrically longer.
T9A03: Polarization = the orientation of the electric field.
T9A04: A handheld's short 'rubber duck' antenna has low efficiency.
T9A06: A Yagi (beam) has the most gain of these.
T9A07: A car body blocks signals from a handheld used inside, so signal strength drops.
T9A08: A quarter wave on 2 m is about 19 inches. Quarter wave in inches = 2808 / MHz, and 2808 / 146 = 19.
T9A09: A 5/8-wave whip has more gain than a 1/4 wave.
T9A10: A dipole radiates strongest broadside, at right angles to the wire.
T9A11: Antenna gain = a stronger signal in one direction compared with a reference antenna.
T9B01: Tape all of these outdoors: PL-259, BNC, and Type N. None of them are waterproof on their own.
T9B03: Coax is the most common feed line because it's easy to use and needs little special care when installing.
T9B04: An antenna tuner matches the antenna system's impedance to the rig's output.
T9B05: Coax loss increases at higher frequencies.
T9B06: Above 400 MHz, use Type N connectors.
T9B07: PL-259s are common at HF and VHF. They aren't waterproof and they aren't bayonet-type.
T9B08: All of these add coax loss: water, high SWR, and extra connectors.
T9B09: Erratic SWR = a loose connection somewhere.
T9B10: RG-213 is thicker than RG-58, with less loss.
T9B11: Air-insulated hardline has the lowest loss.
T9B12: SWR measures how well the load is matched to the feed line.
